cards.title: Meet the musical alphabet
cards.body: Only seven letters: A, B, C, D, E, F, G — then they repeat. Middle C sits near the center of the piano, and every other note is measured from there. Seven letters run all of Western music.

cards.title: Notes have length, not just pitch
cards.body: A whole note holds for 4 beats, a half note for 2, a quarter note for 1, and an eighth note for half a beat. Rhythm is just pitch plus timing — the same note means different things depending on how long you hold it.

Play C D E F as quarter notes — one beat each — and you've played four even steps. Now play them as eighth notes (two per beat) and the same four notes feel twice as urgent. Same pitches, completely different energy.
Count out loud until it clicks: say 1-2-3-4 under quarter notes, 1-and-2-and under eighth notes. Your mouth is the cheapest metronome ever made.

cards.q: How many beats does a half note get?
cards.explain: Half of a whole (4 beats) is 2. Quarter = 1, half = 2, whole = 4 — the names are literally fractions of a whole note.

flashcards.front: How many different note letters are there?
flashcards.back: Seven: A, B, C, D, E, F, G. After G the alphabet wraps back to A, one octave higher.

flashcards.front: How long is a quarter note?
flashcards.back: One beat. It's the default pulse — most music you hear counts in quarter notes.
The speed of the beat, measured in beats per minute (BPM). 120 BPM means two beats every second.
The distance from one note to the next note with the same letter — C to C, for example. It sounds like the 'same' note, higher.

questions.q: After G, what comes next in the musical alphabet?
questions.explain: The musical alphabet only uses A through G, then repeats. After G comes A, one octave up.

questions.q: A whole note lasts 4 beats. How long is an eighth note?
questions.explain: Eighth = 1/8 of a whole note = half a beat. Two eighth notes fit inside a single beat.
BPM = beats per minute. 100 BPM means a beat lands 100 times each minute — a relaxed walking pace.

questions.q: Which lasts longer: a half note, or two quarter notes tied together?
questions.explain: Both total 2 beats. A tie just glues note lengths together — the math is identical.

choices: It sits near the middle of the piano keyboard
It's the middle of every song
It's always played with the middle finger
questions.explain: It's roughly at the center of a standard 88-key piano, and it works as the landmark other notes are measured from.

cards.title: A scale is a ladder of notes
cards.body: A scale is a set of notes in ascending order, defined by the pattern of steps between them. Learn one pattern and you can build that scale starting from any note on the keyboard.

cards.title: Whole steps and half steps
cards.body: The smallest step on a piano is a half step — one key to its immediate neighbor, black or white. Two half steps make a whole step. Every scale is just a recipe of wholes and halves.
C major = all white keys: C D E F G A B C. The pattern is W-W-H-W-W-W-H. No sharps, no flats — that's why C major is where everyone starts.
Sharps (#) raise a note one half step; flats (b) lower it one half step. The same piano key can have two names — C# and Db are the same pitch. Musicians call that an enharmonic.

cards.q: The major pattern is W-W-H-W-W-W-H. Starting on G, what's the 7th note?
cards.explain: Count it out: G(1) A(2) B(3) C(4) D(5) E(6) F#(7). The half step between E and F# forces the sharp — that's why G major has one sharp.

flashcards.back: An ordered set of notes built from a fixed pattern of whole and half steps.

flashcards.front: What is the major scale pattern?
flashcards.back: W-W-H-W-W-W-H: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
Raises a note by one half step. A flat lowers it by one half step.

flashcards.front: How many sharps does C major have?
flashcards.back: None. C major uses only white keys — the only major scale with no sharps or flats.

choices: One piano key to its immediate neighbor
questions.explain: One key to its immediate neighbor — black or white — is a half step. It's the smallest interval in Western music.

questions.q: In C D E F G A B C, where do the half steps fall?
questions.explain: Those pairs have no black key between them on the piano — that's exactly where the H steps of W-W-H-W-W-W-H land.
Same twelve notes, different pattern — the flattened 3rd gives minor its darker color. Happy vs. sad is the quickest way to hear the difference.

choices: The same pitch with two names
questions.explain: One piano key, two spellings — an enharmonic. Which name you use depends on the key you're playing in.

questions.q: How many distinct notes in a major scale (not counting the repeated top note)?
questions.explain: Seven distinct notes, then the octave repeats the starting note — C D E F G A B, then C again.

cards.title: Chords are note stacks
cards.body: Play three or more notes at once and you get a chord. The most common stack — the triad — is built from the 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes of a scale. Stack every other note and harmony appears.

cards.title: Major vs. minor: it's the middle note
cards.body: A major triad has a wide (major) 3rd; a minor triad has a narrow (minor) 3rd. C–E–G sounds bright; C–Eb–G sounds moody. One note moved a half step changes the entire feeling.
Build C major in 3 steps: 1) Take the C major scale: C D E F G A B. 2) Grab the 1st (C), 3rd (E), and 5th (G). 3) Play them together — that's a C major chord.
Roman numerals name chords by position: I, IV, V. Thousands of pop songs are just I–V–vi–IV on repeat. Learn those four shapes and you can fake your way through most radio hits.

cards.q: C minor is C–Eb–G. What changed from C major (C–E–G)?
cards.explain: E to Eb is one half step down. That flattened 3rd is the entire difference between major and minor triads.

flashcards.back: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes of a scale, played together.

flashcards.front: What makes a chord minor instead of major?
flashcards.back: The 3rd is lowered one half step — a minor 3rd instead of a major 3rd.

flashcards.front: What is a I–IV–V progression in C major?
flashcards.back: The C, F, and G chords — the 1st, 4th, and 5th chords of the scale. The backbone of blues and rock.

flashcards.front: How many notes minimum for a chord?
flashcards.back: Three. Two notes played together is just an interval.

questions.q: Which scale degrees form a basic triad?
questions.explain: Root, third, fifth — stack every other note and you get the triad. That's the recipe for every basic chord.

questions.q: G–B–D is what kind of chord?
questions.explain: G to B is a major 3rd (two whole steps) and G to D is a perfect 5th — the major triad recipe.

questions.q: You flatten the 3rd of a major chord. What do you get?
questions.explain: Lowering the 3rd by a half step converts major to minor. Same root, same 5th — new mood.

questions.q: In I–V–vi–IV in C major, what is the vi chord?
questions.explain: The 6th note of C major is A, and the vi chord is minor by default. I–V–vi–IV = C–G–Am–F.

questions.q: Why do songwriters love the I–IV–V progression?
choices: It creates tension and release that feels satisfying
questions.explain: The V chord pulls hard back to I — that tension-and-release is the engine of countless songs, from blues to pop-punk.
